description: Team of students from Specialized Muhammad al-Khwarizmi school.
summary: We built a simulation game, ultramars.vercel.app, in which players create and manage their own civilization. Our goal is to show how life could be sustained on other planets and what resources it would take, while teaching players how to manage those resources. What makes the game matter is less its mechanics than its audience. It teaches children about the intricate aspects of colonization, such as producing oxygen, drilling for ice, mining iron and growing plants. The project will help curious young minds discover astronomy.
details:
Project Details
Mars Colony Command is a 3D strategy game that runs in a web browser. It is made for kids aged 7–12, who lead the first human settlement on Mars. Players start in Jezero Crater, where NASA’s Perseverance rover landed. Their first base has a habitat dome, a solar farm, a life-support plant and a greenhouse with chickens. From there they build roads, mine ice and iron, make oxygen, store power in batteries and keep their crew alive. They also send survey rovers to reveal the planet region by region. As the colony grows, players research new technology in a skill tree, upgrade their orbiter to find buried water, and send crew convoys to found new bases at real landing sites NASA has studied. Nobody arrives from Earth: the population grows on Mars and needs free beds to grow. Players can make an account, save to the cloud, appear on an online leaderboard and visit other players’ bases in 3D.

Benefits and intended impact. Most science lessons ask kids to remember facts. Our game lets them use those facts to make decisions. When a player’s oxygen runs low, they learn that each colonist needs about 0.84 kg of it every sol (a Mars day), and that the MOXIE experiment on Perseverance made oxygen from the carbon dioxide in the Martian air. When they choose a new base site, they weigh the same trade-offs as NASA planners: water ice, radiation, flat ground and sunlight. We want kids to come away seeing that space exploration is about engineering, planning and teamwork, and that they could do that work someday. Nothing in the game is ever destroyed. Problems show up as warnings to fix, so younger players can experiment without being punished.

Tools and technologies. We wrote the game in TypeScript. Three.js draws the 3D planet, Vite builds the project and Zustand holds the game state. The terrain is generated in a Web Worker so the game stays smooth, and it is cached in the browser with IndexedDB. Supabase stores accounts, cloud saves and the leaderboard, with database rules so players only see what they should. We built the detailed 3D buildings and rovers in Blender with Python scripts and exported them as GLB models. We used Vitest for automated tests, Git for version control, and Claude Code, an AI coding assistant, to help write and debug the code. The project is about 23,000 lines of code.

Creativity. The whole Mars globe is drawn in 3D, and more than 40 real landmarks sit at their real coordinates, including Olympus Mons, Valles Marineris, Hellas, Gale and Jezero. The map is split into the 30 official USGS Mars chart regions, and players uncover them one by one. Our pipelines borrow ideas from the Trans-Alaska Pipeline, such as zigzag routes that handle temperature changes and quakes. Research follows NASA’s Technology Readiness Levels, from “concept study” to “mission ready.” Each building has a fun fact that explains the real science behind it.

Factors we considered.
Accuracy: We based the game’s numbers on NASA sources, like the Mars Fact Sheet, the life-support handbook NASA uses to plan crew needs (the BVAD), MOXIE results and orbiter data. We listed more than 40 sources, with links, in a sources file. Where we changed a number to make the game more fun, we marked it as a game value so it isn’t mistaken for real data.
Age-appropriate design: We kept controls simple, used no violence and showed warnings instead of failures.
Safety: Players only share a username. There is no chat or messaging, and we filter usernames. Profiles can be viewed but not contacted, and the leaderboard never shows emails or private data.
Accessibility: The game runs in any modern browser with nothing to install. It has three language modes: English, Uzbek, and Russian.
Performance: We generate and cache terrain in the background so the game runs on school laptops.
